newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Durum wheat crop suffers in France.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Durum wheat crop suffers in France.

text.p: Production of pasta-making durum wheat is predicted to drop by up to a quarter in two of France's key producing zones this year and there are warnings of worse damage as farmers gauge the effects of a spring drought.

Crop analysts and officials the Midi-Pyrenees region in the south, and the Provence-Alpes-Cote d'Azur region in France's southeast, said farmers in some areas would not even bother to harvest while a lucky few had saved their crops by watering.
The regions are the second and third French producing zones for durum respectively, and together make up 49 percent of the 256,840 hectares of land sown to durum this year.
France is the fourth European producer of the pasta grain, which is also exported to North Africa for making couscous.
"The yield forecasts are probably going to come down. It has been a particularly bad year -- really it could not have been worse," a regional crop official in Marseille said.
Current forecasts are for a 26 percent drop in yields in the Midi-Pyrenees region near Toulouse to four tonnes per hectare.
With a small part of the harvest already gathered in the Provence-Alpes-Cote d'Azur region north of Marseille, officials there point to a 21 percent drop in yields to 2.5 tonnes.
But the risk is that yields will fall even further as more of the sun-shrivelled crop is weighed and assessed at silos.

Several farmers are reporting yields of less than two tonnes, levels not seen on any widespread basis in the past 30 years, though it is too early to say yet how many farms are so badly affected, crop analysts said.

Crops suffered as the soil dried after three months without rain between January 15 and April 15. That was followed by a frost. The problems were then compounded by a small tornado in the northern Vaucluse district this month, where several square kilometres of arable land were churned up and destroyed.
"I think we could say we've had everything this year," said an official responsible for the area.

France's huge export-earning grain crop is seen less at risk nationally. Northern grain growers look set to recover from the second successive drought, leading to another big crop after last year's record of 62 million tonnes and keeping prices down.
But for the southeast this year's dry spell threatens damaged harvests and financial difficulties for both producers and the cooperatives that earn money by storing grain.
Southern durum is one of the main crops at risk, though farmers in less subsidised sectors like fruit and vegetables have also seen their harvests badly damaged by drought.
"There are a few farmers who just won't harvest," another local grain official said. "The cost of getting the combine out is more than the value of what is left on the ground."
For others the harvest is ready to start but has ironically been delayed by rain in the past few days -- far too late to help fill out the depleted grain stalks which are already ripe.
